title: Observation of Critical Current Minimum in Super-Honeycomb Josephson Junction Arrays
authors: Melissa Mikalsen, Alexander-Georg Penner, Samuel D. Escribano, Nadav Drechsler, Arunav Bordoloi, Jacob Issokson, Felix von Oppen, Yuval Oreg, Javad Shabani
abstract: Superconductor-semiconductor Josephson junction arrays are a uniquely tunable platform for studying collective quantum phenomena, particularly in the regime where localized Andreev bound states can hybridize across the lattice when the physical separation between adjacent junctions is smaller than their coherence length ($ξ_{\text{ABS}}>d_{\text{JJ}}$). Here, we investigate three distinct Al-InAs Josephson junction arrays: a square array and super-honeycomb array fabricated within this ${ξ_{\text{ABS}}>d_{\text{JJ}}}$ regime, as well as a larger-spacing super-honeycomb control device designed such that $ξ_{\text{ABS}}\lesssim\!~d_{\text{JJ}}$. Under an out-of-plane field, critical current peaks emerge at rational filling factors, reflecting stable vortex configurations in the lattices. In the super-honeycomb lattice, vortices localize to distinct non-identical plaquettes at different filling factors, as predicted by frustrated XY model simulations. A rotating in-plane field yields periodic critical current oscillations that reflect the Rashba spin-orbit coupling inherent to the InAs quantum well. Surprisingly, at $f = 1$, the closely spaced super-honeycomb array exhibits a distinct critical current minimum as the magnitude of the in-plane field increases, a signature absent in the square array and large-spacing super-honeycomb array. These results indicate that this signature is jointly influenced by the unique geometry of the super-honeycomb vortex lattice and by long-range inter-junction hybridization.
summary: This work examines Josephson junction arrays in superconducting semiconductors to study collective quantum behavior influenced by magnetic fields. By comparing square and super-honeycomb geometries, the authors report observing a unique critical current minimum in the closely spaced super-honeycomb array at $f=1$. This finding suggests that long-range inter-junction hybridization is crucial for understanding vortex lattice stability beyond simple XY model predictions.
main_problem: The study investigates collective quantum phenomena, specifically critical current behavior, in superconducting Josephson junction arrays under applied magnetic fields.
main_result: A distinct critical current minimum is observed uniquely in the closely spaced super-honeycomb array at a specific flux filling factor ($f=1$), which cannot be explained by simple XY model physics alone.
method: The research combines magnetotransport measurements of critical current ($I_c$) with numerical simulations based on the frustrated 2D XY model.
model_or_system: The physical system is an Al-InAs Josephson junction array, studied in both square and super-honeycomb geometries. The physics is modeled using a frustrated XY Hamiltonian incorporating Andreev bound states (ABS) hybridization ($\xi_{ABS}>d_{JJ}$) and Rashba spin-orbit coupling.
key_observables: Critical current ($I_c$), vortex localization patterns, resistance vs. bias/field measurements.
important_parameters: Frustration factor ($f = B_{\perp}A_{uc}/\Phi_0$), in-plane field magnitude and angle ($	heta$, $B_{||}$), junction spacing relative to coherence length ($\xi_{ABS}/d_{JJ}$).
main_assumptions: The simple XY model is insufficient, necessitating the inclusion of long-range inter-junction hybridization effects for accurate description.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM images of the arrays and plots detailing $I_c$ vs. perpendicular field (showing vortex peaks) and $R$ vs. $I$ dependence on in-plane field angle ($	heta$) or magnitude ($B_{||}$), highlighting geometry-dependent features.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the platform, compares different geometries (square vs. super-honeycomb), analyzes vortex localization via out-of-plane fields, and then investigates the unique $I_c$ minimum induced by in-plane fields, contrasting theoretical model limitations with experimental observations.
why_interesting: The study probes how geometric frustration and intrinsic spin-orbit coupling interact to create novel quantum signatures (like the critical current minimum) that deviate from standard mean-field models, relevant for understanding topological superconductivity.
